planting.note: Set out container-grown palms in spring so the root system establishes well before the first winter cold snap.

directions: This naturally occurring intergeneric hybrid between Pindo Palm (Butia) and Queen Palm (Syagrus) combines the graceful, arching, feathery queen-palm silhouette with the far superior cold tolerance of its Butia parent, surviving brief drops into the low teens Fahrenheit once established. Plant in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil and water deeply and regularly through the first two to three years while the trunk gains girth and height. Being a sterile hybrid it produces no viable seed, so propagation is only by offset division or tissue culture, and named specimens are grown from a single original tree discovered in Louisiana. Once established it is fast-growing for a cold-hardy palm and tolerates heat, humidity, and periodic drought with minimal maintenance beyond removing spent fronds.

planting.note: Transplant container-grown palms in spring to allow a full growing season for root establishment before cold weather.

directions: Native to the grasslands of Argentina, Uruguay, and southern Brazil, Yatay Palm is the tallest and most stately of the cold-hardy Butia species, eventually forming a thick gray trunk topped with a dense crown of long, stiff, silvery-blue arching fronds. Plant in full sun in well-drained soil; young palms tolerate light shade but develop their best trunk and crown form with full exposure. It is markedly drought tolerant once established but grows fastest with regular deep watering and occasional feeding during the warm season. The small orange-yellow fruits that follow inconspicuous flower spikes are edible and were traditionally used to make jelly, much like the related Pindo Palm.

planting.note: Set out in spring so roots have a full season to establish before facing winter cold.

directions: Native to the highlands of Santa Catarina state in southern Brazil, Woolly Jelly Palm gets its common name from the dense, cottony wool-like fiber that sheaths the flower stalk and persists on the crown, distinguishing it from the more familiar Pindo Palm. It forms a slower-growing, more compact single trunk clad in old leaf-base stubs, topped with stiff, recurved, silvery-gray-green fronds that give strong textural contrast in the landscape. Grow in full sun in well-drained soil; it is notably drought tolerant once established and needs little supplemental water outside of extended dry spells. Small tart-sweet orange fruits ripen in summer and can be used for jelly, following the same culinary tradition as its Butia relatives.

planting.note: Plant in spring from containers; well suited to large pots as well as in-ground planting.

directions: Selected from wild populations found on the small volcanic island of Vulcano off Sicily, this dwarf, densely clumping form of Mediterranean Fan Palm stays far more compact than the species, with shorter internodes and stiffer, silver-backed fan fronds packed into a tight, symmetrical crown. Plant in full sun to light shade in lean, well-drained, alkaline-tolerant soil and avoid overwatering, as it is naturally adapted to rocky, dry coastal conditions. Its slow growth and small ultimate size make it an excellent choice for containers, courtyards, and tight landscape beds where the full-size species would eventually outgrow the space. Once established it needs only occasional deep watering during drought and removal of old fronds at the base of each clump.

planting.note: Set out container-grown plants in spring so roots establish well before the first winter cold snap.

directions: Confirmed by DNA analysis in 2011 as a naturally occurring ancient hybrid between Sabal palmetto and Sabal minor, this exceptionally rare palm survives only in a small pocket of Brazoria County, Texas, near the San Bernard National Wildlife Refuge. It combines an above-ground trunking habit with the cold hardiness of its dwarf palmetto parent, having reportedly come through winter lows near -15°F undamaged, and grows roughly twice as fast as Sabal minor toward its eventual trunked form. Plant in full sun to light shade in average to wet, well-drained soil; it tolerates both periodic flooding and drought once established. Because wild populations are critically limited, seek out nursery-propagated stock only and give it a permanent site, as it resents transplanting once trunk formation begins.
